stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu: CM directs officials to brace for flood in Bapatla district
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: CM directs officials to brace for flood in Bapatla district
stories.summary: Heavy inflows are expected through irrigation canals from upstream districts for four days
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu directed officials to take all precautionary measures to prevent loss of life and property in Bapatla district in view of Cyclone Murasu, which has intensified into a severe cyclonic storm.
He reviewed the preparedness of district administrations through a video conference on Monday (November 2, 2026), attended by Bapatla Collector Vinod Kumar V.

The Chief Minister warned that Bapatla was likely to bear the brunt of the cyclone, since heavy inflows of floodwater were expected through irrigation canals from upstream districts, including Guntur, Palnadu, Prakasam and Markapuram.
He asked officials to inspect canal bunds, remain alert for four days of heavy inflows, evacuate people from low-lying areas and establish rehabilitation centres.
He also said a special officer would be appointed for Bapatla district.
In a review meeting on cyclone preparedness, Mr. Naidu said the District Collectors should be alert to meet any contingency keeping in view the likelihood of heavy rains and gales.
He ordered that steps be taken to fill reservoirs, tanks and ponds through efficient water management in the south coastal and Rayalaseema regions.
Officials told the Chief Minister that heavy rains were expected in south coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema, along with copious inflows into the Nagarjuna Sagar and Pulichintala project catchment areas.
They said the impact of Murasu could be less than that of Cyclone Arnab but necessary precautionary steps were being taken.
Mr. Vinod Kumar said the administration had prepared a comprehensive plan involving all departments.
Rainfall in the district was 30% below normal, but rain was likely for five days.
He said 74 vulnerable locations had been identified, including irrigation canals, roads and tank bunds, where damage was possible.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu: TTD steps up safety measures in Tirumala to ensure hassle-free darshan
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: TTD steps up safety measures in Tirumala to ensure hassle-free darshan
stories.summary: Additional EO directs officials to expedite darshan arrangements, provide sheltered Annaprasadam distribution, monitor vulnerable ghat-road stretches and keep medical teams on alert to ensure pilgrim safety
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: With cyclone Murasu posing a potential threat to pilgrim movement in Tirumala, TTD Additional Executive Officer Ch.

Venkaiah Chowdary on Monday directed officials to step up precautionary measures to ensure uninterrupted darshan, sheltered distribution of food and the safety of devotees throughout their pilgrimage.

Chairing a review meeting with officials of various departments at the Sudharma Meeting Hall in Tirumala, he stressed the need for coordinated efforts to prevent rain-related disruptions and ensure that devotees do not face inconvenience while waiting for darshan or accessing essential facilities.
Officials were directed to expedite darshan arrangements and ensure that queue lines did not extend beyond designated premises, exposing pilgrims to rain.
He also instructed them to erect tarpaulin shelters wherever necessary to facilitate uninterrupted distribution of Annaprasadam.

The Engineering and Electrical Departments were asked to ensure uninterrupted power supply and maintain heightened vigilance along the ghat roads, particularly at stretches vulnerable to rock and boulder falls.
Medical personnel were instructed to remain on alert and provide immediate assistance to devotees who slip or sustain injuries due to rain.

Emphasising inter-departmental coordination, the Additional EO called upon all TTD wings to work in tandem to safeguard pilgrims, facilitate hassle-free darshan and ensure their safe return to their destinations.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu: AP Govt fully prepared, says CM Naidu
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: AP Govt fully prepared, says CM Naidu
stories.summary: The impact of Murasu’s winds could affect around 8,000 electricity poles across the south coastal and Rayalaseema districts; overall impact lower than Arnab
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Cyclone Murasu is likely to have a relatively limited impact on the Andhra Pradesh coast with forecasts indicating lower wind speeds and rainfall intensity compared to Cyclone Arnab, Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu said.

Reviewing the State government’s preparedness for the cyclone from the Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) centre at the Secretariat in Amaravati, the Chief Minister directed senior officials and district collectors to remain on high alert, particularly in the south coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema regions, where moderate to heavy rainfall is expected.
He stressed the need to make effective use of the anticipated rainfall to replenish irrigation tanks and reservoirs while ensuring that there is no loss of life or property.
Officials informed him that 31,000 electricity poles had been dispatched to the field level from Srikakulam to Krishna district following Cyclone Arnab.
The impact of Murasu’s winds could affect around 8,000 electricity poles across the south coastal and Rayalaseema districts.
Another 1,000 personnel are being brought from Chennai to assist with power restoration.
Naidu directed officials to deploy them in Nellore, Prakasam and other affected districts as required.
Officials warned of heavy rainfall in several districts under the influence of Cyclone Murasu.
Palnadu is likely to receive the highest rainfall of around 30 cm, followed by Prakasam (24 cm), Markapuram (19 cm), Krishna and Guntur (9 cm each), and Eluru and Nellore (9 cm each).
The Chief Minister instructed officials to clear drains in advance in areas expected to receive heavy rainfall and remain vigilant in locations vulnerable to overflowing streams and rivulets.
With heavy rainfall forecast in the catchment areas of the Nagarjuna Sagar and Pulichintala projects, officials estimated that inflows could range between 30 TMC and 50 TMC, according to a release.

stories.headline: After Cyclone Arnab, Murasu nears Andhra coast: 20+ flights cancelled, Odisha steps up evacuation
stories.title: After Cyclone Arnab, Murasu nears Andhra coast: 20+ flights cancelled, Odisha steps up evacuation
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Cyclone Murasu is approaching Andhra Pradesh with winds of up to 110 kmph.
Authorities have stepped up evacuations and emergency preparations, while flights have been cancelled and schools shut in parts of Tamil Nadu.
Amaravati: Cyclone Murasu intensified into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal on Monday, November 2, as it moved towards the Andhra Pradesh coast.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast that the system will cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole, around 11.30 pm on Monday and the early hours of Tuesday, November 3.
According to the IMD's latest bulletin cited in the updates, the cyclone is likely to make landfall with sustained wind speeds of 100–110 kmph and gusts reaching up to 120 kmph.
At 11.30 am on Monday, the storm was centred over the west-central Bay of Bengal, approximately 120 km east-southeast of Nellore and 140 km from Kavali.
It had moved west-northwestwards at around 14 kmph over the preceding six hours.
The weather department has also indicated the possibility of Murasu intensifying further into a very severe cyclonic storm before reaching the coast.
Heavy rainfall and strong winds are expected across parts of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha as the system advances.
The Andhra Pradesh government has intensified its preparations ahead of the cyclone's landfall.

Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has directed officials to remain prepared, while Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan held a review meeting with officials from the panchayat raj, rural development and rural water supply departments.
Kalyan asked officials in Nellore, Prakasam, Markapuram, Bapatla and Krishna districts to remain vigilant and arrange the evacuation of people living in low-lying areas to safer locations.

stories.headline: ‘Bada pataka’ under the counter, fake green labels on display: Banned firecrackers flood Delhi markets after Supreme Court nod
stories.title: ‘Bada pataka’ under the counter, fake green labels on display: Banned firecrackers flood Delhi markets after Supreme Court nod
stories.summary: The Hindu finds rockets, bombs and flowerpots sold discreetly in Sadar Bazar and Jama Masjid, with some green-labelled crackers lacking QR codes; vendors cite demand for louder fireworks as police seize over 1,100 kg
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Hours after the Supreme Court permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR on November 7 and 8, traditional firecrackers were being openly sold, albeit discreetly, in Old Delhi’s Sadar Bazar and Jama Masjid markets.

A visit by The Hindu found vendors concealing banned crackers in cartons and black polythene bags beneath displays of green-labelled fireworks, with some selling conventional crackers without the QR codes required to verify their authenticity.
At least 10 vendors approached by The Hindu said traditional firecrackers, referred to in the market as “bada pataka”, were available.

One vendor opened his phone to show photographs of rockets, bombs, flowerpots and ground spinners, along with their prices, and said the items selected by a customer could be brought from a nearby warehouse in “five minutes”.

stories.headline: Jitendra Singh highlights expansion of disaster preparedness, weather monitoring infrastructure with new Seismological Observatory inaugurated in Kishtwar
stories.title: Jitendra Singh highlights expansion of disaster preparedness, weather monitoring infrastructure with new Seismological Observatory inaugurated in Kishtwar
stories.summary: Kishtwar, Nov 2: Inaugurating the new Seismological Observatory in the high seismic zone of Kishtwar today through the Ministry of Earth Sciences, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology, Earth Sciences, Minister of State in the Prime Minister's Office, Department of Atomic Energy and Department of Space, Dr Jitendra Singh today highlighted the significant expansion of meteorological and weather monitoring infrastructure in Jammu & Kashmir after 2014, particularly in the erstwhile Doda district, with additional installations brought in after the Chasoti cloudburst tragedy last year. Addressing the gathering, Dr Jitendra Singh said that the India Meteorology Department (IMD) had strengthened the weather monitoring network in the region from not a single Doppler Weather Radar in 2014 to 4 installed in last 12 years and 4 more being installed making it total 8; Automatic Weather Stations from 3 to 12 out of which 4 for Kishtwar and 2 each for Doda and Ramban. Dr. Srinivasa Kumar Tummala, Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Govt of India, Senior Scientist Suresh and others came specially from Delhi for the event. MLA Padder-Nagseni Constituency and Leader of Opposition, J&K Legislative Assembly, Sunil Sharma; MLA of the Kishtwar Assembly Constituency and Shagun Parihar also spoke on the occasion. Deputy Commissioner Kishtwar, Pankaj Sharma and SSP Kishtwar Sunny Gupta were also present among others. The Minister said, the expansion of scientific and weather monitoring infrastructure has also strengthened the region's disaster preparedness in an area that is vulnerable to earthquakes, landslides and other weather-related challenges. The new observatory at Kishtwar is equipped with state-of-the-art digital seismic equipment and will transmit data in real time to the 24x7 Earthquake Monitoring Centre of the National Centre for Seismology in New Delhi. With the establishment of the new facility, Jammu and Kashmir now has four Seismological Observatories, including those at Jammu, Srinagar, Udhampur and Kishtwar. Dr Jitendra Singh said the observatory would continuously monitor earthquake activity in the region and contribute to a better understanding of its seismic hazards. The information generated would also support the district administration and rescue teams in responding more effectively, besides helping in planning safer infrastructure. Highlighting the transformation in meteorological infrastructure since 2014, Dr Jitendra Singh said that there was no Doppler Weather Radar coverage in the region earlier. After 2014, four Doppler Weather Radars have been installed at Banihal, Jot, Jammu and Srinagar, significantly expanding weather monitoring capabilities. He further informed that four more Doppler Weather Radars are set to be commissioned in 2027 at Doda, Kishtwar, Anantnag and Baramulla, further strengthening weather surveillance and extending coverage across the region. The Minister also highlighted the significant expansion of the Automatic Weather Station network. From three Automatic Weather Stations earlier at Udhampur, Kathua and Ramban, nine additional stations have been added, taking the total number to 12. These include four stations in Kishtwar, two each in Doda and Ramban, and one in Kathua. Dr Jitendra Singh said that the expansion of scientific infrastructure has been guided by the needs and geographical vulnerabilities of the region. He noted that administrative boundaries may change, but geographical challenges remain, making it essential to strengthen weather monitoring and early warning systems across vulnerable areas. The rainfall monitoring network has also been expanded, with the number of Rain Gauge Stations increasing from nine to 15 across the five districts of the parliamentary constituency. The weather forecast and agromet advisory services have reached 5,467 beneficiaries, enabling wider access to weather-related information. He also referred to the strengthening of specialised meteorological facilities in the region, including the High-Altitude Cloud Physics Laboratory at Patnitop, Jammu and Kashmir. The meteorological infrastructure in Jammu has also been strengthened with the establishment of a Regional Meteorological Centre to provide weather and early warning services. Dr Jitendra Singh said that access to timely weather information has made a tangible difference to local administration and disaster preparedness. Referring to recent experiences, he noted that advance weather information helped the district administration plan and manage activities with greater ease. Emphasising the importance of public cooperation, the Minister said that scientific weather warnings can save lives only when they are taken seriously and acted upon. He recalled an instance when traffic restrictions were imposed following a weather alert and subsequent damage to the highway demonstrated the importance of adhering to timely warnings. “Information is important, but following the information is equally important,” he emphasised, calling upon citizens to cooperate with the administration during weather alerts and advisories. Dr Jitendra Singh also spoke about the need to counter unverified and alarmist information with scientific and evidence-based communication. He said that weather-related information and predictions should be understood on the basis of scientific assessment and credible sources. Highlighting the positive potential of technology and social media, the Minister said that access to digital information and new platforms has created opportunities for young people, including those living in remote areas. He urged the youth to make constructive use of the opportunities and facilities now available to them. Dr Jitendra Singh also reflected on the wider transformation of the region, referring to improved connectivity and the development of Kishtwar as a major power hub. He said the region's scientific and infrastructure capabilities were being strengthened alongside efforts to improve the safety and well-being of its people. The event was attended by senior officials, public representatives and other dignitaries.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Grants Bail To Man Accused Of Storing Cow Meat
stories.title: Supreme Court Grants Bail To Man Accused Of Storing Cow Meat
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Observing that having a mere criminal antecedent would not be definitive proof of guilt, the Supreme Court recently granted bail to a man who had five similar criminal antecedents and was accused of procuring 23 kg of cow meat and storing it in an open plot for retail sale purposes.

A bench of Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice Vipul M. Pancholi allowed the appeal filed by Mohammad Aarif Abdul Razak Samol, who had been arrested on January 3, 2026, and remained in custody for more than eight months.
The appellant was booked under Sections 5(1), 6(b), 8(2), 8(4) and 10 of the Gujarat Animal Preservation Act, 2011, Section 325 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), and Section 119 of the Gujarat.
Police Act.
The prosecution alleged that he had illegally procured 23 kg of cow meat, transported it in a Swift car, and stored it in an open plot near his house for retail sale.
It was further alleged that he fled from the spot after the police conducted a raid.
Opposing bail, the State submitted that the trial was at its final stage and would be concluded within two months.
It also pointed out that the appellant had five criminal antecedents involving similar allegations and argued that he was likely to indulge in similar activities if released.
The appellant, however, contended that the prosecution case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence and presumptions.
His counsel submitted that he had not been arrested at the spot, the meat had been recovered from an open plot accessible to everyone, and the plot did not belong to him.
It was also argued that the Swift car allegedly used for transporting the meat was not owned by the appellant.

Finding that the appellant's continued incarceration was not warranted, the Court noted that the alleged meat had been recovered from an open plot near his house, the charge-sheet had been filed and the trial had already commenced.

stories.headline: Five poll-bound states see voter numbers drop after SIR exercise
stories.title: Five poll-bound states see voter numbers drop after SIR exercise
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 2 : The number of voters across Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa, Punjab and Manipur came down by up to 13.24 per cent after the completion of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter list, data shows. The five states will go for assembly polls early next year. According to data made public by the Election Commission and state chief electoral officers in recent past, across these five states, the electorate shrank from about 18.71 crore to 16.43 crore after SIR, a net reduction of around 2.29 crore -- about 12.2 per cent. Uttar Pradesh, which has the biggest electorate among states, alone accounted for nearly 90 per cent of the total drop. In UP, which went for SIR in phase II, the electors went from 15.44 crore pre-SIR to 12.56 crore in the draft roll, then 13.40 crore in the final rolls. The net loss stood at around 2.04 crore or 13.24 per cent, the steepest among the five states. The draft removed about 2.89 crore names, and about 0.84 crore (roughly 29 per cent) were restored. In Punjab, where SIR was held in phase III, the electors went from 2.15 crore to 1.94 crore in the draft, then 2.01 crore in the final rolls. The net loss in the number of voters was about 0.14 crore or 6.34 per cent. It had the strongest recovery. About 0.07 crore of the roughly 0.21 crore draft deletions (about 34 per cent) came back to the rolls. In Uttarakhand, where poll roll revision was held in phase III, electors went from 0.80 crore to 0.71 crore, ending at 0.72 crore. The net loss of voter base was about 0.08 crore or 10.07 per cent. Only about 0.0025 crore returned, around three per cent of draft deletions. SIR was held in phase III in Manipur, where electors went from 0.209 crore to 0.193 crore, and ended at 0.196 crore. The net loss of voters was about 0.013 crore or 6.33 per cent, similar to Punjab. About 17 per cent of draft deletions were restored, the data shows. In Goa, where SIR was held in phase II, the electors went from 0.1185 crore to 0.1085 crore, then fell further to 0.1058 crore. In Goa, the net loss was nearly 0.013 crore or 10.76 per cent. Goa is the only one of the five where the final roll is smaller than the draft, so there was no net restoration. While ordering special summary revision in 17 states recently, the EC had noted that assembly polls in the five states could be held "early next year". The ongoing special summary revision ahead of polls will ensure that left-out voters get a fresh chance to get included in the electoral rolls. The young voters who turn 18 on or before January 1 will get an opportunity to be included as voters and can cast their vote in these five states. While the term of the 403-member UP assembly ends on May 22 next year, the terms of 60-member Manipur, 40-member Goa, 117-member Punjab and 70-member Uttarakhand assembly end on different dates in March 2027. Provisions of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, allow the EC to hold polls "earlier than six months before the term expires". PTI

stories.headline: Gujarat orders schools with 100+ students to hire counsellors
stories.title: Gujarat orders schools with 100+ students to hire counsellors
stories.summary: Gandhinagar, Nov 2: All secondary and higher secondary schools in Gujarat will have to set up dedicated teams to monitor students' mental health and prevent suicides under new regulations introduced by the state government, with schools having 100 or more students required to appoint at least one qualified counsellor. The provisions, which will apply to students of Classes 9 to 12 in schools affiliated with the Gujarat Secondary and Higher Secondary Education Board (GSHSEB), seek to address growing concerns over academic pressure, examination-related anxiety, social media use, family expectations and other factors affecting students' mental well-being. The Education Department has introduced Regulation 16(A) in the Gujarat Secondary and Higher Secondary Education Regulations, 1974, and incorporated detailed provisions in Appendix 8 covering mental health, student welfare and suicide prevention. "The decision was taken under the guidance of Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel, Education Minister Pradyuman Vaja and Minister of State for Education, Rivaba Jadeja," officials said. It follows a Supreme Court judgment laying down 15 binding guidelines and four directives on students' mental health and suicide prevention in educational institutions. The Union Ministry of Law and Justice had instructed states to implement the directions. The state has also adopted the UMMEED guidelines developed by the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) as a reference framework. UMMEED stands for Understand, Motivate, Manage, Empathise, Empower and Develop. Under the new regulations, every school offering Classes 9 to 12 must constitute a School Wellness Team (SWT) at the beginning of each academic year. The team will be responsible for identifying students experiencing mental distress, responding to suicide risks and ensuring timely access to support. Its functioning will be reviewed annually. The school principal will lead the team, while the school counsellor or a designated teacher will serve as its coordinator. It will also include one teacher each from the secondary and higher secondary sections, a School Management Committee representative, a non-teaching staff member and two student peer leaders, known as 'Mano-Mitra', with one each from Classes 9-10 and 11-12. The Mano-Mitra initiative will establish a peer-support system within schools. These student representatives will provide initial emotional support to classmates, guide those requiring help towards appropriate assistance and encourage supportive relationships among students. Schools with 100 or more students must appoint at least one qualified counsellor, psychologist or social worker trained in child and adolescent mental health. Institutions with fewer than 100 students will have to establish formal referral arrangements with external mental health professionals, nearby Community Health Centres and Primary Health Centres, the District Mental Health Programme and Tele-MANAS services. Special mentoring arrangements will also be required during critical transition periods, including board examinations, result announcements and students moving from Class 8 to 9 and Class 10 to 11. Dedicated mentors or counsellors must be assigned to small groups during these periods. The regulations prohibit schools from segregating students inside or outside classrooms on the basis of academic performance, examination results or marks. Students must not be publicly humiliated, compared with their peers or stigmatised over their academic performance. Schools will also be barred from practices that could create anxiety, fear, an inferiority complex or emotional insecurity. Instead, institutions will have to promote an environment based on equality, dignity, encouragement and cooperation. They must regularly organise co-curricular and extracurricular activities such as yoga, meditation, art, music, gardening, dance and sports. Initiatives including Khel Mahakumbh, Finishing School, Saptadhara, Pariksha Pe Charcha, NSS, NCC, Scouts and Guides, and community service have also been included as activities to support students' well-being. Schools must ensure that students can approach counsellors or designated mentor teachers confidentially and without fear to discuss their concerns and emotional difficulties. Help boxes or suggestion boxes must also be made available. Official child helpline numbers and SWT contact details must be displayed prominently on school websites, notice boards, in classrooms, hostels and counselling rooms. The framework makes mental health training mandatory for all teaching and non-teaching staff at least twice a year. The training, to be conducted by certified mental health professionals, will cover psychological first aid, identification of warning signs, responses to self-harm and referral procedures. Any indication of self-harm, suicidal thoughts, severe mental distress or other risky behaviour must be treated seriously and addressed immediately. In the event of a suicide attempt or self-harm incident, the student must not be left alone, and appropriate medical or emergency assistance must be arranged without delay. The regulations also require strict confidentiality of students' mental health information, counselling records and other sensitive personal details. Such information may be shared only with authorised persons directly involved in the student's safety, treatment, counselling or welfare. In the event of a suicide, schools must arrange psychological, emotional and social support for other students, teachers, staff members and affected family members through a postvention process. Communication about the incident must remain factual and responsible. Only the principal or an authorised officer may interact with the media, and details about the method, location, photographs or other sensitive personal information must not be disclosed. Schools will also have to establish confidential and accessible grievance redressal mechanisms to address sexual harassment, ragging, bullying, cyberbullying and discrimination based on caste, class, gender, religion, language, socio-economic status or disability. Complaints must be investigated in a timely and impartial manner. The regulations provide for institutional accountability where a school fails to take timely and appropriate action despite being aware, or reasonably expected to be aware, of a risk situation, and that failure is found to have significantly contributed to serious harm, self-harm or a suicide involving a student. Disciplinary or legal action may be initiated against the school or responsible officials under applicable laws and regulations. To reduce academic and career-related pressure, schools will also be required to provide regular career guidance and information about different educational, vocational, skill-based and entrepreneurship opportunities. A District-Level Monitoring Committee, led by the District Magistrate or District Collector, will oversee the implementation of the regulations. It will review compliance across educational institutions, coordinate guidance, monitor complaints and serious incidents, and recommend corrective measures. All schools will be required to comply with the committee's directives. --IANS

opening: Gandhinagar, Nov 2: All secondary and higher secondary schools in Gujarat will have to set up dedicated teams to monitor students' mental health and prevent suicides under new regulations introduced by the state government, with schools having 100 or more students required to appoint at least one qualified counsellor.

The provisions, which will apply to students of Classes 9 to 12 in schools affiliated with the Gujarat Secondary and Higher Secondary Education Board (GSHSEB), seek to address growing concerns over academic pressure, examination-related anxiety, social media use, family expectations and other factors affecting students' mental well-being.
body: The Education Department has introduced Regulation 16(A) in the Gujarat Secondary and Higher Secondary Education Regulations, 1974, and incorporated detailed provisions in Appendix 8 covering mental health, student welfare and suicide prevention.
It follows a Supreme Court judgment laying down 15 binding guidelines and four directives on students' mental health and suicide prevention in educational institutions.
The Union Ministry of Law and Justice had instructed states to implement the directions.
The state has also adopted the UMMEED guidelines developed by the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) as a reference framework.
UMMEED stands for Understand, Motivate, Manage, Empathise, Empower and Develop.
Under the new regulations, every school offering Classes 9 to 12 must constitute a School Wellness Team (SWT) at the beginning of each academic year.
The team will be responsible for identifying students experiencing mental distress, responding to suicide risks and ensuring timely access to support.
Its functioning will be reviewed annually.
The school principal will lead the team, while the school counsellor or a designated teacher will serve as its coordinator.

It will also include one teacher each from the secondary and higher secondary sections, a School Management Committee representative, a non-teaching staff member and two student peer leaders, known as 'Mano-Mitra', with one each from Classes 9-10 and 11-12.
The Mano-Mitra initiative will establish a peer-support system within schools.
These student representatives will provide initial emotional support to classmates, guide those requiring help towards appropriate assistance and encourage supportive relationships among students.
Schools with 100 or more students must appoint at least one qualified counsellor, psychologist or social worker trained in child and adolescent mental health.

Institutions with fewer than 100 students will have to establish formal referral arrangements with external mental health professionals, nearby Community Health Centres and Primary Health Centres, the District Mental Health Programme and Tele-MANAS services.
Special mentoring arrangements will also be required during critical transition periods, including board examinations, result announcements and students moving from Class 8 to 9 and Class 10 to 11.
Dedicated mentors or counsellors must be assigned to small groups during these periods.
The regulations prohibit schools from segregating students inside or outside classrooms on the basis of academic performance, examination results or marks.
Students must not be publicly humiliated, compared with their peers or stigmatised over their academic performance.
Schools will also be barred from practices that could create anxiety, fear, an inferiority complex or emotional insecurity.
Instead, institutions will have to promote an environment based on equality, dignity, encouragement and cooperation.
They must regularly organise co-curricular and extracurricular activities such as yoga, meditation, art, music, gardening, dance and sports.

Initiatives including Khel Mahakumbh, Finishing School, Saptadhara, Pariksha Pe Charcha, NSS, NCC, Scouts and Guides, and community service have also been included as activities to support students' well-being.
Schools must ensure that students can approach counsellors or designated mentor teachers confidentially and without fear to discuss their concerns and emotional difficulties.
Help boxes or suggestion boxes must also be made available.
Official child helpline numbers and SWT contact details must be displayed prominently on school websites, notice boards, in classrooms, hostels and counselling rooms.
The framework makes mental health training mandatory for all teaching and non-teaching staff at least twice a year.
The training, to be conducted by certified mental health professionals, will cover psychological first aid, identification of warning signs, responses to self-harm and referral procedures.
Any indication of self-harm, suicidal thoughts, severe mental distress or other risky behaviour must be treated seriously and addressed immediately.
In the event of a suicide attempt or self-harm incident, the student must not be left alone, and appropriate medical or emergency assistance must be arranged without delay.
The regulations also require strict confidentiality of students' mental health information, counselling records and other sensitive personal details.
Such information may be shared only with authorised persons directly involved in the student's safety, treatment, counselling or welfare.
In the event of a suicide, schools must arrange psychological, emotional and social support for other students, teachers, staff members and affected family members through a postvention process.
Communication about the incident must remain factual and responsible.
Only the principal or an authorised officer may interact with the media, and details about the method, location, photographs or other sensitive personal information must not be disclosed.

Schools will also have to establish confidential and accessible grievance redressal mechanisms to address sexual harassment, ragging, bullying, cyberbullying and discrimination based on caste, class, gender, religion, language, socio-economic status or disability.
Complaints must be investigated in a timely and impartial manner.

The regulations provide for institutional accountability where a school fails to take timely and appropriate action despite being aware, or reasonably expected to be aware, of a risk situation, and that failure is found to have significantly contributed to serious harm, self-harm or a suicide involving a student.
Disciplinary or legal action may be initiated against the school or responsible officials under applicable laws and regulations.

To reduce academic and career-related pressure, schools will also be required to provide regular career guidance and information about different educational, vocational, skill-based and entrepreneurship opportunities.
A District-Level Monitoring Committee, led by the District Magistrate or District Collector, will oversee the implementation of the regulations.
It will review compliance across educational institutions, coordinate guidance, monitor complaints and serious incidents, and recommend corrective measures.
All schools will be required to comply with the committee's directives.
--IANS.
